name: Enzacamene

lead: Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an organic UVB filter that was used in sunscreens, especially in Europe, to reduce sunburn and the photodamage behind sunspots and wrinkles.

It absorbs UVB and dissipates the energy partly through cis-trans isomerisation, though its photostability is described as limited. Regulators moved against it after lab and animal studies reported estrogenic and thyroid effects, and the EU SCCS found sufficient evidence of endocrine disruption in 2022. Appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

paras: It appeared as one ingredient among several filters in SPF products. Today it mostly comes up when people check ingredient lists and regional availability; it remains permitted in some countries, such as Canada, while the EU banned it in cosmetics in 2024 and the US never approved it.

Lab and animal studies reported estrogenic and thyroid effects, and human studies detected it in plasma, urine and milk. It is banned in EU cosmetics and reportedly in the UK and China, and is not FDA-approved.

angle.text: Enzacamene (4-MBC) is an older camphor-derived UVB filter that was used in sunscreens to cut sunburn and the photodamage that leads to sunspots and wrinkles. It is now banned in EU cosmetics, so it mainly comes up when people check ingredient lists. Appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

lead: Enzacamene (4-methylbenzylidene camphor, 4-MBC) is a camphor-derived organic UVB filter that has been used in sunscreens and SPF-labelled skincare [1]. By absorbing UVB radiation before it reaches the skin, filters like this contribute to the sun protection that helps keep skin tone even and limits the visible effects of sun exposure, which is why it appears on ingredient lists of some facial and body products.

It has been the subject of endocrine-activity research, and it has been banned in cosmetics in the European Union (Regulation (EU) 2024/996), with further bans reported in the UK and China [1]. It remains permitted in some places, including Canada (up to 4%) and Australia; it is not FDA-approved in the United States [1]. It is discussed in sunscreen-ingredient communities mainly in the context of ingredient safety and regional availability.

Research on the compound includes in vitro and rodent studies of estrogenic and thyroid effects, human absorption studies, measurements in breast milk, and environmental monitoring in lakes, rivers and fish. [1][2][3][4][5][6]

paras: Enzacamene is a white crystalline powder, insoluble in water, with a melting point of about 66 to 69 degrees Celsius. It absorbs UVB radiation and is used in sunscreens and in skincare products that claim an SPF value. [1] It is one of several organic filters reviewed in dermatology literature on sunscreen choices and changing regulations. [7][8]

Enzacamene is a water-insoluble white crystalline solid that dissipates absorbed UV energy partly through cis-trans isomerisation; its low quantum yield (0.13 to 0.3) for that process suggests other photochemical reactions occur, which is linked to limited photostability [1]. Formulation research has examined carriers such as solid lipid microparticles and microspheres to influence how the filter penetrates or stays on the skin. [9][10]

In vitro work reported estrogenic activity for several UV filters including 4-MBC, which displaced estradiol from estrogen receptor beta and increased uterine weight in immature rats [2]. Reporter-gene assays also examined 4-MBC interactions with estrogen, androgen and progesterone receptors [11]. Wikipedia reports lower thyroid hormone, higher TSH and enlarged thyroid glands in rodents at higher doses, and altered estrogen-responsive genes after developmental exposure in rats [1].

A human study measured systemic absorption after whole-body topical application of benzophenone-3, octyl methoxycinnamate and 4-MBC, alongside reproductive hormone levels [3]. Another reported UV filters in human plasma and urine after repeated whole-body application [4]. 4-MBC has also been detected in human milk, with levels correlated with cosmetic use [5]. The EU's scientific committee concluded in 2022 that genotoxicity data were insufficient, and a review of endocrine-disrupting properties of UV filters discusses the broader literature. [1][12]

Studies have detected 4-MBC in wastewater, surface water and fish in Swiss lakes [6][13] and in surface waters in several countries [14]. A review of environmental effects of sunscreen ingredients discusses it among other filters [15].
No clinical trials of enzacamene as a cosmetic or sunscreen treatment were found. Human data consist of absorption and exposure studies [3][4][5] and a registered photopatch study of UV filters [16].

Denmark proposed warnings against use in children under 12 in 2001, and retailers there largely stopped selling products containing it; a 2013 Danish assessment confirmed endocrine-disrupting properties and a 2015 survey found it absent from Danish cosmetics [1]. The EU Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety concluded in 2022 that endocrine-disruption evidence was sufficient and genotoxicity data insufficient [1].

Regulation (EU) 2024/996, adopted 3 April 2024, moved 4-MBC to the list of prohibited cosmetic substances; products could not be placed on the market from 1 May 2025 and could not be made available from 1 May 2026 [1]. In the UK, regulations were laid on 15 January 2026, with placing on the Great Britain market barred from 15 July 2026 and existing stock sellable until 14 January 2027; Northern Ireland follows EU rules [1]. China moved 4-MBC from permitted (previously up to 4%) to prohibited in January 2026 [1]. Palau banned it nationwide from 1 January 2020 and Thailand restricts it in national parks [1]. Canada permits it up to 4%, Australia permits it in therapeutic sunscreens, and it is not approved in the US or Japan [1].
